noun:November.tx: Inherited from Middle High German november.

intj:nu.tx: From Middle High German nu, nuo. The form without a final -n remained common in some dialects and was reinforced by German Low German nu, from Middle Low German nû.

adv:nicht.tx: From Middle High German niwiht, niweht, niht, a contracted form of Old High German niowiht, from Proto-West Germanic *naiwwiht. Essentially from nio (“never”) + wiht (“being, creature”), the last from Proto-Germanic *wihtą.

intj:nicht.tx: From Middle High German niwiht, niweht, niht, a contracted form of Old High German niowiht, from Proto-West Germanic *naiwwiht. Essentially from nio (“never”) + wiht (“being, creature”), the last from Proto-Germanic *wihtą.

num:null.tx: From the noun Null (“the number zero”), from Italian nulla, from Latin nulla, feminine singular of nullus (“no, none”).

adj:null.tx: From the noun Null (“the number zero”), from Italian nulla, from Latin nulla, feminine singular of nullus (“no, none”).

adv:null.tx: From the noun Null (“the number zero”), from Italian nulla, from Latin nulla, feminine singular of nullus (“no, none”).

verb:nerven.tx: From Nerv (“nerve”) via the expression auf die Nerven gehen (“to get on (someone's) nerves”).

adv:ne.tx: From Middle High German ne, ni (“not, if not”), from Old High German ne, ni (“no, not, not at all, by no means”), from Proto-West Germanic *ne, from Proto-Germanic *ne (“not”), from Proto-Indo-European *né (“not”). Also possibly from a contraction of nicht, dialectal net, nit, ni.

intj:na.tx: Perhaps from an unstressed form of nu. Compare also Swedish nå, Russian ну (nu), Finnish no, and their cognates.

adj:nah.tx: Inherited from Middle High German nāh, from Old High German nāh. Compare English nigh. Doublet of nach.

adv:nah.tx: Inherited from Middle High German nāh, from Old High German nāh. Compare English nigh. Doublet of nach.

num:neunzehn.tx: From Middle High German niunzëhen, from Old High German niunzehan, from Proto-Germanic *newuntehun. Equivalent to neun + zehn. Compare Dutch negentien, English nineteen, Danish nitten.

noun:Nike.tx: From Ancient Greek Νίκη (Níkē), from νίκη (níkē, “victory”).

noun:Nachtwächter.tx: From Middle High German nahtwahter, from Old High German nahtwahtāri, from Proto-West Germanic *nahtawahtāri. Equivalent to Nacht (“night”) + Wächter (“guardian”). Cognate with Dutch nachtwachter and West Frisian nachtwachter.

noun:Nilpferd.tx: From Nil (“Nile”) + Pferd (“horse”), a loose calque of Latin hippopotamus, from Ancient Greek ἱπποπόταμος (hippopótamos). Akin to Dutch nijlpaard.

intj:nix.tx: A widespread form in dialects all over the German language area, probably the same as standard nichts, that is, a contraction of it.

noun:Nacht.tx: Inherited from Middle High German naht, from Old High German naht, from Proto-West Germanic *naht, from Proto-Germanic *nahts, from Proto-Indo-European *nókʷts.

prep:nach.tx: From Middle High German nāh, from Old High German nāh with preservation of word-final -h as -ch; thus pertaining to modern nah (“near”) (from Old High German inflected nāh-), from Proto-West Germanic *nāhw, from Proto-Germanic *nēhw. Cognate with Dutch na, English nigh.

adv:nach.tx: From Middle High German nāh, from Old High German nāh with preservation of word-final -h as -ch; thus pertaining to modern nah (“near”) (from Old High German inflected nāh-), from Proto-West Germanic *nāhw, from Proto-Germanic *nēhw. Cognate with Dutch na, English nigh.

verb:nehmen.tx: Inherited from Middle High German nëmen, from Old High German nëman, from Proto-West Germanic *neman, from Proto-Germanic *nemaną, from Proto-Indo-European *nem- (“to give or take one's due”). Cognate with Low German nehmen (“to take”), Dutch nemen (“to take”), English nim (“to take, filch”), Danish nemme (“to learn, grasp”), Swedish förnimma (“to perceive”). More at nim, the native English …

noun:Narr.tx: From Middle High German narre, from Old High German narro, further etymology unknown. Cognates include Yiddish נאַר (nar), Bavarian Noar, German Low German Narr, Dutch nar, West Frisian nar, Saterland Frisian Naar, Danish nar, Swedish narr.

verb:nebeln.tx: From Middle High German nebelen, nibelen, from Old High German nibulen.

noun:Nebel.tx: From Middle High German nëbel, from Old High German nëbul, from Proto-Germanic *nebulaz, from Proto-Indo-European *nébʰos (whence also Proto-Balto-Slavic *nébas, Proto-Indo-Iranian *nábʰas, Ancient Greek νεφέλη (nephélē, “cloud, mist”), Latin nebula (“mist, fog”)). More at English nuel.

noun:Neffe.tx: From Middle High German neve, from Old High German nefo, nevo, from Proto-West Germanic *nefō, from Proto-Germanic *nefô. Cognate with Dutch neef, obsolete English neve. Further from Proto-Indo-European *népōts, whence English nephew, which see for more. The form with -ff- is irregular and was spread by Luther. The development -v- → -ff- before a sonorant (here the n of the inflected forms) is …

intj:nein.tx: From Middle High German nein, from a contraction of Old High German ni ein. Compare Old English nān, from ne ān (Modern English none, further contracted to no).

adj:neu.tx: From Middle High German niuwe, from Old High German niuwi, from Proto-West Germanic *niwi, from Proto-Germanic *niwjaz, from Proto-Indo-European *néwos. Compare Dutch nieuw, English new, Danish ny, Gothic 𐌽𐌹𐌿𐌾𐌹𐍃 (niujis).

pron:nichts.tx: From Middle High German nihtes niht (“nothing of nothing”), a reenforcing construction with niht. Compare French rien de rien, Spanish nada de nada. See nicht. Cognate with Dutch niets, Low German nix, Hunsrik nichs.

adv:nie.tx: From Middle High German nie, from Old High German nio.

adj:nackt.tx: From Middle High German nacket, from Old High German nackut, from Proto-Germanic *nakwadaz, from Proto-Indo-European *nogʷós (“naked, bare”). Cognate with Low German naakd, Dutch naakt, English naked, Danish nøgen, Swedish naken.

adv:nur.tx: From late Middle High German nuor, contracted from older niwer, newære, from Old High German niwāri, ni wāri (“were it not”). Cognate with Yiddish נאָר (nor), Dutch maar, Old English nǣre.

conj:nur.tx: From late Middle High German nuor, contracted from older niwer, newære, from Old High German niwāri, ni wāri (“were it not”). Cognate with Yiddish נאָר (nor), Dutch maar, Old English nǣre.

adj:nebelig.tx: From Middle High German nebelic, from Old High German nebulīg. Equivalent to Nebel + -ig.

adv:nun.tx: From Middle High German nu, nū, nuo with a secondary final -n, already occasionally in Middle High German nuon, from Old High German nu, from Proto-West Germanic *nū.

intj:nun.tx: From Middle High German nu, nū, nuo with a secondary final -n, already occasionally in Middle High German nuon, from Old High German nu, from Proto-West Germanic *nū.

conj:nun.tx: Clipping of nun dass or nun da.

adj:national.tx: Borrowed from New Latin nātionālis and influence of French national.

adj:neutral.tx: 16th century, borrowed from Latin neutralis, at first in political parlance.

noun:Nase.tx: From Middle High German nase, from Old High German nasa, from Proto-West Germanic *nasu, from Proto-Germanic *nasō, from Proto-Indo-European *néh₂s. Compare Low German Nees, Norwegian nese, English nose.

prep:neben.tx: Inherited from Middle High German nëben, enëben, from Old High German in ëbanī. Cognate with Dutch neven, compare also English anent.

adj:nobel.tx: Borrowed from French noble, from Latin nobilis.

num:neunzig.tx: From Middle High German niunzec, from Old High German niunzug, from Proto-West Germanic *neun tigiwi. Equivalent to neun + -zig.

adj:nonchalant.tx: Borrowed from French nonchalant, from Old French nonchaloir, from Latin non (“not”) + calēre (“to be warm”).

noun:Nagel.tx: From Middle High German nagel, from Old High German nagal, from Proto-West Germanic *nagl.

noun:Name.tx: From Middle High German name, from Old High German namo, from Proto-West Germanic *namō. Cognate with Dutch naam, Low German Naam, Alemannic German Name, Yiddish נאָמען (nomen), English name, West Frisian namme, Danish navn, Swedish namn.

noun:Natter.tx: From Middle High German nātere, from Old High German nātara (first attested in the 8th century), from Proto-West Germanic *nadrā. Doublet of Otter “adder, viper”.

noun:Natur.tx: Inherited from Middle High German natūre, from Old High German natūra, ultimately from Latin nātūra.

noun:Nazi.tx: 1924, representing the pronunciation of Nati- in Nationalsozialist (“National Socialist”), influenced by Sozi (“socialist”), as pejorative possibly also influenced by Nazi, a Bavarian hypocorism of Ignatius.

noun:Neger.tx: Borrowed from French nègre, ultimately from Latin niger. Cognate with Hunsrik Negher.

noun:Neige.tx: From Middle High German neige. See neigen (“to slope”).

noun:Nest.tx: From Middle High German nest, from Old High German nest, from Proto-West Germanic *nest, from Proto-Germanic *nestą, from Proto-Indo-European *nisdós.

noun:Neutrum.tx: Borrowed from Latin neutrum (“neither, neuter”), neuter singular of neuter.

noun:Nickel.tx: A pet form of the proper masculine name Nikolaus, see also Old Nick "the devil", Nickel, and Nicholas. See Kupfernickel for more.

noun:Niet.tx: From Middle High German nieten, from Old High German hniotan, from Proto-West Germanic *hneudan, from Proto-Germanic *hneudaną.

noun:Niveau.tx: Borrowed from French niveau. Doublet of Level and Libelle.

noun:Nix.tx: From Middle High German niches, nickes, from Old High German nihhus, nichus, from Proto-Germanic *nikwus, *nikwis, from Proto-Indo-European *nigʷ-ō-s, from Proto-Indo-European *neygʷ- (“wash”). Cognate with Old English nicor.

noun:Nord.tx: From Middle High German nort, from Old High German nord, from Proto-West Germanic *norþr.

noun:Not.tx: From Middle High German nōt, from Old High German nōt, from Proto-West Germanic *naudi. Cognates * Low German Nood * Dutch nood * English need * Danish nød * Icelandic nauð.

noun:Note.tx: Ultimately from Latin nota (“mark, sign, remark, note”).

noun:Nu.tx: Substantivisation of nu (“now”), alternative form of nun (“now”).

noun:Nuance.tx: Borrowed from French nuance (“nuance, shade, hue”).

noun:Null.tx: Since late 16th c. From earlier form Nulla (c. 1500), from Italian nulla, from Latin nūlla, feminine of nūllus (“no one”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *né, *óynos and *-lós.

verb:nennen.tx: From Middle High German nennen, nemmen, nemnen, from Old High German nemnen, from Proto-West Germanic *namnijan, from Proto-Germanic *namnijaną. Cognates Cognate with Hunsrik nenne, Old English nemnan, Middle English nemnen, Swedish nämna.

adj:niedlich.tx: An originally Low and Central German word from Middle Low German nǖtlīk (“delicious, delicate”) and Central Franconian Middle High German nītlīche, late Central Middle High German niethlīchen (“eagerly”). It is then from Old Saxon niudlīko (“eagerly”) (compare Old English nēodlīċe), Proto-West Germanic *niudi (“desire, eagerness”), equivalent to nied + -lich. More at English needly.

verb:nachlassen.tx: From Late Middle High German nāchlāȥen. Equivalvent to nach- + lassen. Cognates include Dutch nalaten and Hunsrik nohlosse.

noun:Nuss.tx: From Middle High German nuȥ, from Old High German nuȥ, from Proto-West Germanic *hnut, from Proto-Germanic *hnuts. Compare Dutch noot, English nut, Danish nød, Swedish nöt.

phrase:nicht die Bohne.tx: Literally, “not the bean”, or more loosely translated as “not even as much as a little seed”.

num:neun.tx: From Old High German niun, from Proto-Germanic *newun, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁néwn̥. Cognate with German Low German negen, Low German negen, Dutch negen, English nine, West Frisian njoggen, Danish ni, Gothic 𐌽𐌹𐌿𐌽 (niun).

noun:Nachtisch.tx: From nach + Tisch. The latter is used here in the otherwise archaic/obsolete sense “meal”.

noun:Nelke.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German nēgelke(n) (“little spike, nail”), from Old Saxon nagal (“nail”). Doublet of Nägelchen and Nägelein (archaic). Low German-looking forms are already found in Middle High German negelkīn alongside negelīn; the contraction is first attested in Central German Nelekin. The feminine form in -e is a backformation from the plural. The name is due to the typical form of …

noun:Napf.tx: From Middle High German naph, from Old High German hnaph, from Proto-West Germanic *hnapp. Cognate with Dutch nap, English nappy.

noun:Netz.tx: From Middle High German netze, from Old High German nezzi, from Proto-West Germanic *nati. Akin to Dutch net, Low German Nett, English net, Danish net, Swedish nät.

noun:Netzwerk.tx: From Netz + Werk. Cognate with English network.

adj:nördlich.tx: Nord + -lich. Cognate to German Low German nördlik (Paderbornisch), Hunsrik nordlich.

noun:Nonne.tx: From Middle High German nunne, from Old High German nunna, from Medieval Latin nonna. The -o- is the regular outcome of Middle High German -u- before a nasal geminate, though it might have been reinforced by relatinisation.

noun:Nudel.tx: Attested since 16th century, further origin unknown. Perhaps from a variant of Knödel, such as Silesian East Central German Knudel. The unusual loss of k- is apparently attested in West Flemish noedel (“dumpling”). If already Middle Dutch, such a dialectal form might have been brought to eastern Germany by Flemish settlers. (Standard Dutch noedel stems from the German.) An alternative theory …

noun:Nadel.tx: From Middle High German nādele, from Old High German nādala, from Proto-West Germanic *nāþlu. Cognate with Dutch naald, English needle, Old Norse nál.

noun:Nachteil.tx: nach- + Teil, formed as an antonym of Vorteil (“advantage”).

adv:noch.tx: From Middle High German noch, nog, from Old High German noh, from Proto-West Germanic *noh, from Proto-Germanic *nuh, from Proto-Indo-European *nu (“now”) + *-kʷe (“and, also”). Cognate to Dutch nog and noch (which are etymologically the same word).

conj:noch.tx: From Middle High German noch, nog, from Old High German noh, from Proto-West Germanic *noh, from Proto-Germanic *nuh, from Proto-Indo-European *nu (“now”) + *-kʷe (“and, also”). Cognate to Dutch nog and noch (which are etymologically the same word).

noun:Niete.tx: From early modern Dutch niet (“nothing”). Compare contemporary niets.

noun:Nessel.tx: From Middle High German neȥȥel, neȥȥele, from Old High German neȥȥila, from Proto-West Germanic *natilā, from Proto-Germanic *natǭ (“nettle”), of unknown origin. Cognate with English nettle, Dutch netel.

noun:Nachbar.tx: From Middle High German nāchbūr, nāchbūre, nāchgebūr, nāchgebūre, from Old High German nāhgibūr, nāhgibūro, from Proto-West Germanic *nāhwagabūrō, from Proto-Germanic *nēhwagabūrô (“neighbour”). Equivalent to nah, nach (“near, next, after”) + Bauer (“dweller, farmer”). The first component underwent pre-cluster shortening, the second was monophthongized from Early Modern German Baur (and then …

pron:niemand.tx: From Middle High German nieman, from Old High German nioman; equivalent to nie (“never”) + Mann (“man”). Cognate with Dutch niemand, Afrikaans niemand, Low German nemann, nemand, nümand, Hunsrik nimmand.

verb:nummerieren.tx: From Latin numerare, from numerus and -are, and from -ieren. Cognate with Hunsrik numereere.

noun:Nummer.tx: From earlier Numero, from Italian numero, from Latin numerus (“number”). The feminine gender is probably due to the influence of Zahl f (“number”).

verb:nagen.tx: From Middle High German nagen, from Old High German nagan, gnagan, from Proto-Germanic *gnaganą. Cognate with English nag and gnaw.

noun:Nacken.tx: From Middle High German nacke, from Old High German *hnahho, from Proto-West Germanic *hnakkō, from Proto-Germanic *hnakkō (“nape, neck”), from Proto-Indo-European *knog-, *kneg- (“back of the head, nape, neck”).

noun:Nabe.tx: From Middle High German nabe, from Old High German naba, from Proto-West Germanic *nabu, from Proto-Germanic *nabō (“nave”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃nebʰ- (“nave, hub”).

noun:Nabel.tx: From Middle High German nabel, nabele, from Old High German nabalo, from Proto-West Germanic *nabulō, from Proto-Germanic *nabalô, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃nóbʰōl.

noun:Nass.tx: From Middle High German and Old High German naz (compare Dutch nat), from Proto-West Germanic *nat, from Proto-Germanic *nataz.

adj:nass.tx: From Middle High German naȥ, from Old High German naȥ, from Proto-West Germanic *nat, from Proto-Germanic *nataz (“wet”), from Proto-Indo-European *ned- (“to be wet”). Cognate with Dutch nat (“wet”), Ancient Greek νοτέω (notéō, “to be wet”), νότος (nótos, “the south wind”).

noun:Nässe.tx: From Middle High German neȥȥe, from Old High German naȥī; analysable as nass + -e.

prep:nächst.tx: See nächster. Compare the Dutch preposition naast (“next to”).

noun:Nähe.tx: From Middle High German næhe, from Old High German nāhī; analysable as nah + -e (“ness”); cognate with Hunsrik Neh.

verb:nähen.tx: From Middle High German nāian, from Old High German nājen, nāian, from Proto-Germanic *nēaną. Cognate with German Nadel and English needle.

verb:nähren.tx: From Middle High German nerren, from Old High German nerien, from Proto-West Germanic *naʀjan, from Proto-Germanic *nazjaną. Cognate with Middle Dutch neren ("to feed", "to provide for oneself"; obsolete Dutch generen).

noun:Nachtigall.tx: Inherited from Middle High German nahtegal, nahtegale, from Old High German nahtagala, from Proto-West Germanic *nahtigalā (literally “she who sings during the night”). Related to Nacht and gellen. Middle High German unstressed -eg- regularly yields modern -ig- (compare the suffix -ig and words like Bräutigam). Cognate with Dutch nachtegaal, English nightingale (which see for more).

noun:Narbe.tx: From Middle High German narwe, from late Old High German narwa (“closed wound”, literally “constriction, narrowness”), from Proto-West Germanic *naru, from Proto-Germanic *narwaz. See also English narrow, Dutch naar.

noun:Nichte.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German nichte, from Old Saxon *nifta, from Proto-Germanic *niftiz. This form replaced High German (obsolete) Niftel in the 17th century. It is based on the Low German shift -ft-→ -cht- (compare Gerücht); hence cognate with Old High German nift, nifta, Dutch nicht, English nift. Related to German Neffe (“nephew”). More at nift, neve.

noun:Neid.tx: From Middle High German nît, from Old High German nīd, from Proto-West Germanic *nīþ.

noun:Nerz.tx: From older Nörz, from Upper Sorbian nórc (“mink”), originally meaning "diver", from Proto-Slavic *nora (“den, lair”), *noriti (“to dive, duck”).

noun:Niere.tx: From Middle High German niere (“kidney; testicle”) m, from Old High German nioro (“kidney; testicle”) m, from Proto-Germanic *neurô m, from Proto-Indo-European *négʷʰrō. The feminine gender is due to the frequent use of the plural, but spread from northern varieties southward; compare Middle Low German nēre f (also Middle Dutch niere f). Cognate with Dutch nier, Danish nyre, Swedish njure, and …

adj:nüchtern.tx: From Middle High German nüehtern, from Old High German nuohtarn, nuohturn, from Latin nocturnus (“nocturnal”). The word was probably originally used among monks in monasteries, with sense development "nocturnal" > "of dawn (the edge of night and day)" > "not having consumed any sustenance yet" > "sober". Compare Danish nøgtern, Hunsrik nichter, English nocturnal.

noun:Nisse.tx: From Middle High German nizze (13th c.), from the plural of older niz, from Old High German niz, from Proto-Germanic *hnits.

verb:niesen.tx: From Middle High German niesen, from Old High German niosan, from Proto-West Germanic *hneusan, from Proto-Germanic *hneusaną, a variant of *fneusaną. Cognate with Dutch niezen, Yiddish ניסן (nisn), English sneeze.

verb:nicken.tx: From Middle High German nicken, from Old High German nicchen, a causative gemination of the ancestral verb to neigen (“to bend, turn”); see the latter for more (DWDS).

adj:niedrig.tx: From nieder + -ig; probably either borrowed or calqued from Middle Low German nēderich. Cognate to Dutch nederig (“humble”).

adj:nieder.tx: From Middle High German nider, from Old High German nidar, from Proto-West Germanic *niþer, from Proto-Germanic *niþer, from Proto-Indo-European *niter. Cognates include English nether, Dutch neder, Luxembourgish nidder, Swedish neder (more commonly ned, ner).

adv:nieder.tx: From Middle High German nider, from Old High German nidar, from Proto-West Germanic *niþer, from Proto-Germanic *niþer, from Proto-Indo-European *niter. Cognates include English nether, Dutch neder, Luxembourgish nidder, Swedish neder (more commonly ned, ner).

prep:nahe.tx: From Middle High German nāch, from Old High German nāh. Cognate with Dutch na, English nigh.

adj:natürlich.tx: From Middle High German natiurlich, from Old High German natūrlīh. Equivalent to Natur + -lich. Compare Dutch natuurlijk, English naturally, Swedish naturlig.

adv:natürlich.tx: From Middle High German natiurlich, from Old High German natūrlīh. Equivalent to Natur + -lich. Compare Dutch natuurlijk, English naturally, Swedish naturlig.

noun:Nashorn.tx: From Nas- (“nose”) + Horn (“horn”), a calque of Ancient Greek ῥινόκερως (rhinókerōs).

noun:Nutte.tx: Originally meant “young girl, young prostitute” in the dialect of Berlin. Further origin unsettled. Possibly from Middle Low German not, nōte (“nut”) in the sense of “vulva, vagina” (compare German Nuss, which has this sense in hunter's jargon); or from Nut (“furrow”), also in the aforementioned sense, but less probably, since this word is not Low German. An alternative hypothesis considers it a …

verb:neigen.tx: From a merger of Middle High German nīgen (intransitive, strong) and neigen (transitive, weak), from Old High German nīgan and neigen, from Proto-Germanic *hnīganą and its causative *hnaigijaną. Cognate with Dutch nijgen and neigen, Old English hnīgan and Old English hnǣgan, Old Norse hnīga and hneiga. Strong forms have been absent from the standard language since the 16th century, but survive in some dialects.

noun:Neumond.tx: Compound of neu (“new”) + Mond (“moon”). Cognate with Hunsrik Neimond, Luxembourgish Neimound.

noun:Nagetier.tx: 18th century, from nagen (“gnaw”) + Tier (“animal”), after earlier Nager, a calque of Latin rodens.

noun:Nachmittag.tx: nach + Mittag. Compare Dutch namiddag, Alemannic German Nomitag.

adj:namentlich.tx: Name (“name”) + -n- + -lich (adverbial and adjectival suffix), with epenthesis of "t" (as e.g. in eigentlich).

adv:namentlich.tx: Name (“name”) + -n- + -lich (adverbial and adjectival suffix), with epenthesis of "t" (as e.g. in eigentlich).

noun:Niederschlag.tx: Deverbal from niederschlagen. Also analysable as nieder- + Schlag.

adj:nützlich.tx: From Middle High German nützelich, from Old High German nuzzilīh (“useful”), equivalent to Nutzen + -lich. Compare Hunsrik nitzlich, Old English nytlīċ.

noun:Nachfrage.tx: Deverbal from nachfragen. Also analysable as nach- + Frage.

adj:notwendig.tx: An early modern German formation: Not (“need”) + wendig (“maneuverable, agile”), originally “necessary to avert the distress”, compare die Not abwenden.

adj:nötig.tx: From Middle High German nœtic, nœtec, nōtic, nōtec, nōdic, from Old High German nōtag (“forced, urgent, needy”), from Proto-West Germanic *naudag (“obligatory, needful”), from Proto-Germanic *naudagaz, equivalent to Not + -ig. Cognate with German Low German nödig, English needy, Swedish nödig.

adv:nötig.tx: From Middle High German nœtic, nœtec, nōtic, nōtec, nōdic, from Old High German nōtag (“forced, urgent, needy”), from Proto-West Germanic *naudag (“obligatory, needful”), from Proto-Germanic *naudagaz, equivalent to Not + -ig. Cognate with German Low German nödig, English needy, Swedish nödig.

verb:necken.tx: Intensive form of nagen (“to gnaw”), with semantic shift “to gnaw” → “to torment” → “to tease”.

pt: character in Greek mythology who became obsessed with his own reflection
noun:Narzissmus.tx: Haplology of earlier Narzissismus. Coined by Sigmund Freud from Narziss (“character in Greek mythology who became obsessed with his own reflection”) + -ismus.

noun:Nikolaus.tx: Borrowed from Latin Nīcolāus. Compare English Nicholas.

adv:nimmer.tx: From Middle High German niemer, from Old High German niomēr, itself usually derived from ni- (“not”) + iomēr (“ever”), thus the same construct as English ever and never. Pfeifer instead derives it from Old High German nio (“never”) + iomēr (modern German nie + immer). The modern (chiefly southern) interpretation, finally, makes it equivalent to a contraction of ni(ch)t mehr (“no more”) or nie …

adj:naiv.tx: From French naïf, from Latin nativus.

adj:nett.tx: From Middle Dutch net (“neat, decent, pretty”), from Old French net (“neat, decent”), from Latin nitidus. Compare English neat.

noun:Narzisse.tx: Borrowed from French narcisse (“narcissus”), from Latin narcissus, from Ancient Greek νάρκισσος (nárkissos).

adv:nachts.tx: From Middle High German nahtes, from Old High German nahtes, equivalent to Nacht (“night”) + -s (adverbial suffix), analogical form to tags. Cognate with English nights (adverb).

conj:nachdem.tx: Equivalent to nach dem, an inflected form which has been used together as a conjunction from Old High German nâh diu.

noun:Nektar.tx: From Ancient Greek νέκταρ (néktar), from Proto-Indo-European *néḱtr̥h₂, derived from the roots *neḱ- (“to perish, disappear”) and *terh₂- (“to overcome”).

noun:Nachricht.tx: Ca. 1600, deverbal from nach + richten. Compare Dutch naricht.

verb:nörgeln.tx: Of Central German origin. According to Pfeifer, from an onomatopoeic Proto-Indo-European *(s)nur- (“to grumble”), along with schnarchen, schnarren, and schnurren, and cognate with Dutch nurken (“to growl”), as well as, outside Germanic, Lithuanian niauróti (“to hum”), niurnė́ti (“to murmur, growl”), snarglỹs (“nasal mucus”), Latvian nurrāt (“to purr”), nirgt (“to show one's teeth”), nerkstēt (“to whine, moan”).

verb:nachfolgen.tx: From Middle High German nāchvolgen, from Old High German nāhfolgēn, from Proto-West Germanic *nāhwafolgēn. Equivalent to nach- + folgen. Cognate with Dutch navolgen.

noun:Necessaire.tx: First attested in the 18th century. Borrowed from French nécessaire.

adj:nervös.tx: From Latin nervōsus, equivalent to Nerv + -ös.

verb:notlanden.tx: Back-formation from Notlandung, equivalent to Not + landen.

adj:neugierig.tx: Compound of neu (“new”) + gierig (“greedy”), but originally neusgierig with an adverbial genitive. A Middle Low German formation that replaced older Middle High German niugerne. Compare Dutch nieuwsgierig and Norwegian Bokmål nysgjerrig.

adv:neugierig.tx: Compound of neu (“new”) + gierig (“greedy”), but originally neusgierig with an adverbial genitive. A Middle Low German formation that replaced older Middle High German niugerne. Compare Dutch nieuwsgierig and Norwegian Bokmål nysgjerrig.

adv:nichtsdestotrotz.tx: Blend of nichtsdestoweniger + trotzdem. Originally humorous and colloquial, but penetrated into the standard register by the second half of the 20th century. Already in 1958, a textbook remarks on existing usage in a serious context. In the DWDS newspaper corpus, it overtook the earlier standard nichtsdestoweniger in usage around 1990, and has become the dominant term since. By surface analysis, …

adv:nichtsdestoweniger.tx: Univerbation of nichts desto weniger. Calque of Latin nihilōminus.

noun:Niederlage.tx: From Middle High German niderlāge. By surface analysis, deverbal from niederlegen.

verb:nachkommen.tx: From Middle High German nāchkomen, from Old High German nāhqueman, nāhkweman, from Proto-West Germanic *nāhwakweman; equivalent to nach- + kommen. Compare Dutch nakomen, Hunsrik nohkomme.

verb:nieseln.tx: Of unclear origin, perhaps from a nasal-initial variant of rieseln (“to sprinkle, trickle”).

noun:Nerv.tx: From Latin nervus, partly via French nerf.

verb:nageln.tx: From Middle High German nagelen, from Old High German nagalen, negilen, from Proto-West Germanic *naglijan, from Proto-Germanic *naglijaną. Equivalent to Nagel + -n.

verb:nachdenken.tx: nach- + denken; cognate with Hunsrik nohdenke, Dutch nadenken.

adj:neblig.tx: From Middle High German nebelic, from Old High German nebulīg. Equivalent to Nebel + -ig.

verb:nieten.tx: From Middle High German nieten, from Old High German *niotan, *hniotan, from Proto-West Germanic *hneudan, from Proto-Germanic *hneudaną.

verb:nahen.tx: From Middle High German nāhen, equivalent to nah (“near”) + -en.

noun:Nachkomme.tx: From Middle High German [Term?]. Compare Hunsrik Nohkommer.

adv:niemals.tx: From nie + -mals. Similar to Dutch niemaals.

noun:Nabelschnur.tx: 18th century, from Nabel (“navel”) + Schnur (“cord, string”). In Old and Middle High German, the word for “navel” was used in this sense on its own, though it is possible that similar compounds were already formed on occasion.

verb:naschen.tx: From Middle High German naschen, from Old High German nascōn (“to nibble; smack”), from Proto-West Germanic *hnaskwōn (“to make soft; tenderize; crush; grind”). Cognate with English nesh (“to soften; act timidly”) and English nosh (“snack”). More at nesh.

noun:Nachwort.tx: nach + Wort. Calque of Ancient Greek ἐπίλογος (epílogos).

noun:Notar.tx: From Middle High German noder, notære, notarje, from Old High German notāri, from Latin notārius.

noun:Nahrung.tx: From Middle High German narunge, from Old High German narunga. By surface analysis, nähren (“to feed”) + -ung (“-ing”). Cognate with Dutch nering.

verb:nähern.tx: From Middle High German næhern. Synchronically derived from nahe. Compare English near (verb).

adv:nirgends.tx: From Middle High German niergent, niergen, neirgen, from ne + irgen, iergen, iergent. Compare German Low German nargens, nargends, Dutch nergens, West Frisian nearne, Saterland Frisian nargends, Old English nāhwærn, nāwern.

adj:nächster.tx: From Old High German nāhisto, from Proto-Germanic *nēhwist (“nearest, closest”). Compare Dutch naast, English next, Danish næste, Swedish nästa.

verb:nutzen.tx: From Middle High German nutzen, nützen, from Old High German nuzzōn, -nuzzen (in ginuzzen), from Proto-Germanic *nutōną, *nutjōną, *nutjaną. Compare modern Nutzen (noun). The verb is originally restricted chiefly to Upper German and East Central German, the former preferring the form nutzen, the latter preferring nützen. By way of hypercorrection, nützen has now become a chiefly southern form. …

prep:nebst.tx: Shortened from earlier nebens, nebenst, nebest, from Middle Low German nēvens, nēvenst, derived from nēven, cognate of German neben (“next to”).

noun:Neider.tx: From Middle High German nīdære, equivalent to Neid (“envy”) + er.

noun:Narwal.tx: Borrowed from Danish narhval or Swedish narval, from Old Norse náhvalr, from nár (“corpse”) + hvalr (“whale”).

verb:niederschlagen.tx: From Middle High German niderslahen, from Old High German nidarslahan. Equivalent to nieder- + schlagen.

noun:Novelle.tx: From Italian novella, from Latin novella.

noun:Nostalgie.tx: Borrowed from New Latin nostalgia, from Ancient Greek νόστος (nóstos, “a return home”) + ἄλγος (álgos, “pain, suffering”), translating German Heimweh.

noun:Neuerung.tx: From Middle High German niuwerunge; by surface analysis, neuern + -ung, the former component from neu.

verb:nippen.tx: In the standard language since the 17th century. From Central and Low German dialects, respectively from northern Middle High German *nippen and Middle Low German nippen, from a Proto-West Germanic *hnipp-Vn, expressive variant of *hnīpan (“to pinch”). Cognate with older Upper German nipfen, Dutch nippen, Old Norse hnippa.

noun:Nebelhorn.tx: From Nebel (“fog”) + Horn (“horn”). The common noun is a kind of horn (honk) used in foggy conditions. The mountain looks like a horn (protrusion) and is often covered in fog.

verb:nachahmen.tx: nach- + ahmen, the latter from Middle High German āmen (“to gauge”), from Middle High German āme, ōme (“liquid measure”), borrowed from Latin ama, hama (“firebucket, pail”), ultimately from Ancient Greek ἄμη (ámē, “water-bucket”).

adj:naseweis.tx: Middle High German nasewīse, by surface analysis, Nase + weis, originally of tracking dogs, transferred sense similar to nosy (“meddlesome”).

noun:Nixe.tx: From Middle High German nixe, from Old High German nicchessa, feminine form of nichus, nihhus (“water-spirit”), from Proto-Germanic *nikwus, *nikwis, perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *neygʷ- (“to wash”). More at nix, nicker.

noun:Nachwuchs.tx: From nach- + Wuchs, formed as the noun to nachwachsen, since the 19th century.

noun:Naht.tx: From Middle High German nāt, from Old High German nāt, from Proto-Germanic *nēdiz, derived from *nēaną (“to sew”), whence German nähen. Cognate with Dutch naad, Low German Nahd.

verb:nachgehen.tx: From Middle High German nāchgān, from Old High German nāhgān, from Proto-West Germanic *nāhwagān. Equivalent to nach- + gehen. Cognate with Dutch nagaan and Hunsrik nohgehn.

adj:neunte.tx: From Middle High German niunte, from Old High German niunto, from Proto-West Germanic *neundō, from Proto-Germanic *newundô. Equivalent to neun + -te.

noun:Nächstenliebe.tx: From nächsten + Liebe. Compare Dutch naastenliefde.

noun:Nickname.tx: Borrowed from English nickname; in pronunciation and inflection sometimes influenced by German Name.

noun:Nüster.tx: 18th century, from Low German Nüster, from Middle Low German nüster, noster. Related to Nase (“nose”).

verb:neiden.tx: From Middle High German nīden, from Old High German nīdōn, from Proto-Germanic *nīþijaną.

verb:nölen.tx: From Low German nölen, whence also Dutch neulen, Danish nøle. The sense "gripe" is derived from "speak slowly or lengthily", itself perhaps from "dawdle" (though it might be the other way round). Further origin uncertain, but usually considered onomatopoeic.

noun:Neusprech.tx: From neu and a deverbal of sprechen as a calque of English Newspeak. First attested in 1949 in reviews of George Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-Four, preceding even an official German translation of the book. By surface analysis, neu + Sprech.

verb:nisten.tx: From Middle High German nisten, from Old High German nisten, synchronically analyzed as a verbal formation related to Nest (“nest”).

verb:nachvollziehen.tx: nach- + vollziehen. First attested in the mid-20th century.

intj:nanu.tx: Borrowed from German Low German na (“well”) + nu (“now”).

phrase:'n Appel und 'n Ei.tx: Literally, “an apple and an egg”. From Low German and/or Central German; see Appel (“apple”). On farms, apples and eggs were often the most numerous produce, so they were very cheap. Cognate with Dutch een appel en een ei.

noun:Nachen.tx: From Middle High German nache (“small boat”), from Old High German nahho, from Proto-Germanic *nakwô. Cognates include Dutch aak (“barque”), Old English naca and Old Norse nǫkkvi

verb:nötigen.tx: From Middle High German nōtigen, from Old High German nōtigōn. Equivalent to nötig + -en.

adv:nahezu.tx: Univerbation of nahe (“near”) + zu (“to”). First attested in the 18th century.

noun:Natron.tx: Borrowed from French natron. Ultimately from Egyptian nṯrj: R9

verb:nachmachen.tx: From nach- + machen. Cognate with Hunsrik nohmache.

verb:notieren.tx: From Middle High German notieren, from Latin notō.

verb:niederlegen.tx: From Middle High German niderlegen, from Old High German nidarleggen, from Proto-West Germanic *niþerlaggjan. Equivalent to nieder- + legen.

adj:notgeil.tx: From Not (“need, distress, emergency”) + geil (“horny, sexually aroused”).

verb:nuscheln.tx: Potentially onomatopoetically influenced variation of Nase + -eln, originally "to speak nasally" (compare näseln).

adj:närrisch.tx: Derived from Middle High German nerrisch, from Old High German nerrisk. By surface analysis, Narr + -isch.

noun:Nahme.tx: From Middle High German nāme, from Old High German nāma, from Proto-Germanic *nēmō.

noun:Narkotikum.tx: Borrowed from Medieval Latin narcōticum (“narcotic”, neuter singular), from Ancient Greek ναρκωτικός (narkōtikós), from ναρκόω (narkóō, “to numb”).

noun:Numerale.tx: Borrowed from Latin numerāle, neuter singular of numerālis.

noun:Neues.tx: Nominalization of neu (“new”); compare Low German Nigges (Paderbornisch, Sauerländisch).

intj:nebbich.tx: From Yiddish נעבעך (nebekh), from Czech nebohý.

adj:nikotinsüchtig.tx: From Nikotin (“nicotine”) + süchtig (“addicted”), equivalent to Nikotinsucht + -ig.

noun:Nachschub.tx: 15th century construction from nach + Schub. Synchronically analyzable as deverbal from nachschieben.

adv:nachgerade.tx: From Middle Low German nā rāde, nā gerāde (“gradually”).

noun:Niednagel.tx: Borrowed from German Low German Niednagel, either from unattested Middle Low German [Term?] or from Dutch nijnagel, nijdnagel (attested as nijnnaghel, 1562). The words may originally be derived from Dutch nijpen, knijpen (“to nip, pinch”). The later form with -d- is due to the belief that such and other harms are caused by other people's envy (Dutch nijd, German Low German Nied, German Neid); …

noun:Neuter.tx: From Neutrum or Latin neutrum by removing the Latin ending -um and inserting an e.

adj:niederträchtig.tx: From Middle High German niderträhtic (“low, looked down upon, disdained”), nidertrehtic. Analyzable as nieder- + -trächtig.

phrase:noch ist Polen nicht verloren.tx: Calque of Polish jeszcze Polska nie zginęła (“Poland is not lost yet”), a famous line from the Polish national anthem. Compare Swedish än är inte Polen förlorat.

verb:niederlassen.tx: From Middle High German niderlāȥen, from Old High German nidarlāȥan. Equivalent to nieder- + lassen.

noun:Nichtsnutz.tx: From German zu nichts nutzen (“be of no avail”).

noun:Nut.tx: From Middle High German nuot, from Old High German nuot (“groove”), from the root of Proto-Germanic *hnōjaną (“to smooth, join together”), from Proto-Indo-European *kneh₂- (compare Ancient Greek κνάω (knáō, “to scratch, scrape”), whence English acnestis).

verb:nachlaufen.tx: From Middle High German nāchloufen, from Old High German nāhloufan, from Proto-West Germanic *nāhwahlaupan; equivalent to nach- + laufen. Cognate with Hunsrik nohlaafe and Dutch nalopen.

verb:netzen.tx: From Middle High German netzen, from Old High German nezzen, from Proto-Germanic *natjaną (“to wetten”).

noun:Nock.tx: Borrowed from German Low German [Term?] meaning “the protruding end of something,” or Dutch nok. Compare English nook, Faroese nakkur (“steep, protruding promontory”).

verb:nachfahren.tx: From Middle High German nāchvarn, from Old High German nāhfaran. Equivalent to nach- + fahren; cognate with Hunsrik nohfaare.

adj:nachtragend.tx: Literally, “carrying after”. From the phrase einem etwas nachtragen (“to hold a grudge against someone for something”, literally “to carry something after someone”).

adj:nagelneu.tx: From Middle High German nagelniuwe, equivalent to Nagel (“nail”) + neu (“new”) implying a recent manufacture or assembly.

adj:nebulös.tx: 19th century, from French nébuleux, from Latin nebulosus. By surface analysis, Nebel + -ös (with a change -el > -ul- as in Fabel → fabulieren etc.).

adj:neunmalklug.tx: From neunmal + klug, literally “nine times clever”.

adj:nullachtfünfzehn.tx: From null + acht + fünfzehn, literally “zero eight fifteen”, from the name of MG 08/15, an early machine gun and standard issue for German soldiers during World War I.

verb:nachholen.tx: 17th century, from nach- + holen, literally “to fetch [something] after”.

noun:Nachtschatten.tx: From Middle High German nahtschate, from Old High German nahtscato; equivalent to Nacht (“night”) + Schatten (“shadow, shade”) (see those entries for more), apparently applied to the plant in reference to its dark flowers and berries; compare English nightshade.

noun:Nachspielzeit.tx: Analysable as nach (“after”) + Spiel (“game”) + Zeit (“time”) or as nachspielen (“to re-play, to make up for missed play”) + Zeit (“time”).

noun:Niedertracht.tx: Back-formation from niederträchtig. Related with tragen in the archaic sense “to behave” (compare betragen). Not related with trachten (“to seek, strive”), though it may now be associated with it (“mean, base striving”, as it were).

verb:nässen.tx: From Middle High German netzen, from Old High German nezzen, from Proto-West Germanic *nattjan, equivalent to nass + -en. Cognate with Middle Low German netten, Dutch netten, English netting (“urine”).

verb:nachlesen.tx: nach- + lesen; cognate with Hunsrik nohlese

adj:nackig.tx: Alteration of now archaic nackicht, itself an alteration of Middle High German nacket.

noun:Nordmanntanne.tx: Nordmann + Tanne, named after Finnish biologist Alexander von Nordmann (1803–1866).

noun:Nonplusultra.tx: Borrowed from Latin nōn plūs ultra. Doublet of Non Plus Ultra.

noun:Nimmerwiedersehen.tx: From nimmer (“never”) + wieder (“again”) + sehen (“to see”) or nimmer + Wiedersehen.

noun:Narretei.tx: A contraction of Narrenteiding, from Narr (“fool”) + -en- + Teiding, from Middle High German teidinc (“chatter”), from Old High German tagadinc (“negotiation”). See the etymology of verteidigen for more.

noun:Nachtwache.tx: From Middle High German nahtwache, from Old High German nahtwahha, from Proto-West Germanic *nahtwaku. Equivalent to Nacht + Wache. Cognate with Dutch nachtwake and Old English nihtwacu. Also related to Dutch nachtwacht and West Frisian nachtwacht (compare Nachtwacht), and English nightwatch.

noun:Nesthäkchen.tx: From earlier Nesthöckelchen, from Nesthocker, from Nest (“nest”) + hocken (“to sit, squat”) + -er. In the contemporary form reanalysable as Nest + Häkchen (“little hook”).

phrase:nach Adam Riese.tx: Named after German mathematician Adam Ries (1492–1559).

verb:niederkommen.tx: From Middle High German niderkomen, from Old High German nidarkweman. Equivalent to nieder- + kommen.

phrase:nach mir die Sintflut.tx: Calque of French après moi le déluge.

verb:niederfallen.tx: From Middle High German nidervallen, from Old High German nidarfallan, from Proto-West Germanic *niþerfallan. Equivalent to nieder- + fallen.

noun:Nichtskönner.tx: From nichts (“nothing”) + Könner (“expert, adept, master”), literally “nothing-can-doer”.

noun:Nordmann.tx: From Middle High German nortman, from Old High German nordman. Equivalent to Nord + Mann. Cognate with Old English Norþmann, Old Norse norðmaðr.

noun:Nachtwächterstaat.tx: Nachtwächter (“night watchman”) + Staat (“state”); coined by German socialist Ferdinand Lassalle in an 1862 speech in Berlin. He used this term to criticize the idea of a state with minimal government, comparing it to a night watchman whose sole duty was preventing theft.

noun:Notdurft.tx: From Middle High German notdurft, from Old High German notthurft. The first element is Not (“need”), while the second is obsolete Durft, which ultimately derives from Proto-Germanic *þurftiz. Also compare dürftig (“sparse, meager”).

verb:neppen.tx: Borrowed from Rotwelsch (thieves' slang) neppen, nappen (“to cheat, pluck someone”). This is possibly a variant of noppen (“to pluck out wool nodules after weaving”).

noun:Nationalstaat.tx: national (“national”) + Staat (“state”), coined in 1842 by the Württemberg liberal politician Paul Pfizer, popularised after the 1848 revolutions.

noun:Neunauge.tx: From Middle High German niunouge, from Old High German niunouga (ca. 900). Equivalent to neun (“nine”) + Auge (“eye”), after the orifices near the head. Compare Dutch negenoog, Danish niøje, Norwegian Nynorsk niauge, Swedish nejonöga. All of these are attested much later and thus probably from German (or Middle Low German).

verb:nießen.tx: From Middle High German nieȥen, from Old High German nioȥan, from Proto-West Germanic *neutan.

noun:Novum.tx: Learned borrowing from Latin novum, since the 18th century.

intj:nagut.tx: Univerbation of na (“well, so”) + gut (“fine, good”), written as one word due to a shift in the pronunciation to a pattern only used in compounds.

noun:Non.tx: Latin nōna (sc. hōra) (“ninth (sc. hour)”); cognate with English noon, nones (“ninth hour”)

noun:Nieswurz.tx: From Middle High German niesewurz, from Old High German nioswurz, hnioswurz, equivalent to niesen (“sneeze”) + Wurz (“herb”) due to its use as a herbal remedy against sneezing fits. Compare English sneezewort (“hellebore”), Dutch nieskruid (“hellebore”).

phrase:nachts ist es kälter als draußen.tx: Literally, “at night it’s colder than outside”.

noun:Noppe.tx: Late Middle High German, from Middle Low German noppe, from Old Saxon *hnoppo, from Proto-Germanic *hnuppô (“knot in a fabric; tuft or flock of wool”). Compare Dutch nop, Swedish noppa.

phrase:nich' lang schnacken, Kopp in'n N.tx: Literally, “no lengthy talking, [get your] head into the nape of [your] neck”.

noun:Nacktbaden.tx: nackt (“naked”) + Baden (“bathing”), gerund of baden (“to bathe”).

verb:normalisieren.tx: Normal + -isieren, after French normaliser, since the 19th century.

noun:Neckermann.tx: Noun sense from Neckermann Reisen, a German budget tour operator.

phrase:niemand hat die Absicht.tx: After the famous statement Niemand hat die Absicht, eine Mauer zu errichten (“No one has the intention to build a wall”), made by East German leader Walter Ulbricht at a press conference in June 1961, two months before the construction of the Berlin Wall.

noun:Nachbrenner.tx: From nachbrennen + -er; equivalent to nach + Brenner.

noun:Neugestaltung.tx: From neu + Gestaltung; equivalent to neugestalten + -ung.

adj:narrisch.tx: From Bavarian narrisch, from Middle High German nerrisch, from Old High German nerrisk.

noun:Njet.tx: Nominalisation of njet, from Russian нет (net).

noun:Nocken.tx: See the etymology of the corresponding lemma form.

phrase:nichts geht mehr.tx: Calque of French rien ne va plus.

intj:njam.tx: Onomatopoeic. Compare English yum and the translations there.

phrase:noch so'n Spruch, Kieferbruch.tx: Literally, “another remark like that, [and you’ll have a] broken jaw”. Attested in printed sources since ca. 1980.

noun:Nagelprobe.tx: From Nagel + Probe, referring to the Daumennagel (“thumbnail”).

verb:niederhauen.tx: From Middle High German niderhouwen, from Old High German nidarhouwan. Equivalent to nieder- + hauen.

verb:niedersetzen.tx: From Middle High German nidersetzen, from Old High German nidarsezzen. Equivalent to nieder- + setzen.

verb:niedermachen.tx: From Middle High German nidermachen. Equivalent to nieder- + machen.

verb:niederstrecken.tx: From Middle High German niderstrecken, from Old High German nidarstrekken. Equivalent to nieder- + strecken.

verb:noppen.tx: From Middle High German noppen (“to form/pick nubs”). Equivalent to a denominal of Noppe (“nodule, bobble”)

noun:Notunterkunft.tx: From Not (“need”, as in "in need") + Unterkunft (“accommodation, lodging”).

adv:nächtens.tx: From Nacht + -ens; or else Nächten with adverbial -s.
